facts.claim: HarperCollins lists the revised Multipliers edition with an on-sale date of May 16, 2017.
facts.mechanism: Because edition date controls which added material is included, the May 16, 2017 listing separates the revised source from the 2010 original.
facts.commonError: Treating every Multipliers edition as identical.
facts.whyWrong: The revised edition adds material that the original release did not include, so edition matters.

facts.claim: The revised edition describes data from more than 150 leaders.
facts.mechanism: Because the model is presented as a research-backed leadership pattern, the 150-plus-leader base matters more than a single anecdote.
facts.commonError: Assuming the framework comes from one memorable executive story.
facts.whyWrong: The publisher describes a broader research base, not one isolated biography.

facts.claim: The central contrast is between Diminishers who drain intelligence and Multipliers who amplify it.
facts.mechanism: Because leader behavior changes whether other people contribute ideas, the contrast is about usable group intelligence rather than politeness.
facts.commonError: Reducing the contrast to mean boss versus nice boss.
facts.whyWrong: A pleasant leader can still diminish if the team's thinking is not needed or used.

facts.claim: The five Multiplier disciplines are presented as learnable skills and practices.
facts.mechanism: Because learnability makes the model actionable, a leader can improve by changing routines rather than waiting for personality change.
facts.commonError: Believing only naturally charismatic leaders can multiply others.
facts.whyWrong: The publisher explicitly frames the disciplines as practices people can learn.

facts.claim: The HBR article appeared in the May 2010 issue under both Liz Wiseman and Greg McKeown.
facts.mechanism: Because the public article predates the 2017 revision, it verifies the original leadership contrast behind the later edition.
facts.commonError: Assuming the revised edition invented the Diminisher and Multiplier distinction.
facts.whyWrong: The distinction was already public in the May 2010 HBR article.

facts.claim: The original release is cataloged as a June 15, 2010 HarperCollins title with ISBN 9780061964398.
facts.mechanism: Because original bibliographic data prevents mixing the revised edition with the first publication record.
facts.commonError: Using the 2010 ISBN as if it proves the 2017 revised contents.
facts.whyWrong: The 2010 ISBN identifies the original edition, not the added revised material.

facts.claim: The productivity claim is doing more with fewer resources by using the intelligence already around the leader.
facts.mechanism: Because unused capability is a resource already paid for, better leadership can raise output without adding headcount first.
facts.commonError: Thinking Multipliers are mainly about employee happiness.
facts.whyWrong: Engagement matters, but the model is also an operating claim about capability and results.

facts.claim: A Diminisher can be highly intelligent and still lower the team's total intelligence in use.
facts.mechanism: Because over-centering one person's answers can stop others from contributing judgment, individual brilliance can reduce collective contribution.
facts.commonError: Assuming the smartest person automatically makes the smartest team.
facts.whyWrong: Team intelligence depends on participation and ownership, not just the leader's IQ.

facts.claim: A Multiplier effect is measured by behavior around the leader, not by the leader's self-image.
facts.mechanism: Because the relevant evidence is whether other people think harder and own more work after interaction with the leader.
facts.commonError: Calling oneself empowering while still making every key decision alone.
facts.whyWrong: Self-description does not prove amplification; observable team contribution does.

allowedAnchors.label: Multiplier effect
allowedAnchors.text: A leader creates a multiplier effect when people around the leader contribute more judgment, initiative, and learning than they normally would under tighter control. The effect is behavioral: questions, challenge, debate, and ownership change how much talent becomes productive work. Internalizing the effect shifts a manager away from being the main source of answers. The practical goal becomes raising the intelligence available in the room, not proving individual superiority.
